The app has no account or service that copies the aggregate elsewhere. A best kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies game progress, not a backup of the browser's accumulated bests or selected-size history.

The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. A developer can inspect or change storage manually, but those are debugging actions rather than product controls.

## Retention and capacity are related, but different

A bounded collection makes its record count predictable. It does not guarantee every write succeeds: browser access can be blocked before capacity matters, and another application on the same origin may consume storage. A small value can fail to write even though its own size is well below a browser's nominal limit.

Conversely, a successful write does not prove indefinite lifetime. The browser can later clear data, a private context can end, or the person can remove site storage. Those environmental conditions are outside the saved-list retention operation. Private browsing notes describes how a value can survive a reload yet disappear when the browsing session ends.

The current score aggregate illustrates the same separation at a smaller scale. It has a naturally small set of keys and bounded integer values, yet `setItem` remains inside a `try` block. Capacity savings reduce the amount being written; they do not change the need to continue play if the browser refuses it.

## Checking retention with feature records

The existing test suite establishes preference behavior rather than a list API. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. Browser journeys check that completed bests survive reloads and game resets. None of those tests asserts a sequence of saved feature records.

For a feature-list review, concrete before-and-after examples can expose the retention boundary without adding fields to the product format. Records can be identified by the already defined domain representation in that feature's tests. The useful observation is which accepted records are present after a save, compared with the preceding accepted collection. Examples can use the feature's existing record fields.

It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. Storage testing guide describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

## What bests retain

The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.

Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to collections, while the current aggregate remains documented and tested according to its own source behavior.
# Storage failure policy

This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.

The current game isolates storage failures from the active game. It catches errors while obtaining the browser store, reading the preference key and writing its replacement. The session can hold its selected size and best results in memory even when no durable write succeeds. There is no current preference-storage warning in the rendered game.

## Features with saved records

For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.

The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.

The existing status display remains driven by session state. A best achieved during a visit can appear there after a failed write because it is already in `session.preferences`. A visible best is evidence of the in-memory result; persistence across a later reload needs separate evidence. Persistence overview describes the data boundary.

## Three browser operations can fail independently

The first operation is acquiring the storage object. `browserStore` in `src/game/session/use-saved-preferences.ts` returns `window.localStorage` inside a `try` block. If the property getter throws, the function catches the exception and returns `null`. A denied property getter is tested in `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` by defining a getter that throws a `SecurityError` before the game initializes.

The second operation is reading the key. A browser can expose an object whose `getItem` later throws. `readPreferences` protects that call and returns `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` on failure. Its optional call also accommodates a `null` store. A successful read can return no value, a malformed string or valid preferences; those are separate outcomes from a thrown read.

The third operation is writing a serialized replacement. `writePreferences` encloses both serialization and `setItem` in its `try` block. A thrown error is swallowed so it cannot interrupt play. A browser may accept reads and refuse writes, so successful startup does not establish successful saving. Quota exhaustion is one possible write failure; browser policy is another.

These stages explain why a single boolean based on the existence of the storage property would be a weak diagnostic. The game doesn't use such a probe. It attempts the real operation at the boundary and catches failure there.

## What the current fallback preserves

Storage failure does not bypass the game's own rules. Card eligibility, move counting, matching, elapsed time and completion still use their normal state transitions. The fallback affects the initial preference value and the durability of subsequent changes. It does not substitute a different deck algorithm or change how many moves a result takes.

After a denied startup read, the game starts at the default size with no saved bests. Choosing another supported size updates the active session. Completing a game can produce a best for that size in memory. New Game and Restart preserve those in-memory preferences because `replaceGame` copies the session preference object rather than rereading the browser store.

If storage remains unavailable, a page reload starts another session from the fallback. The earlier in-memory best is gone with the old page. This is the expected consequence of unsuccessful saving, even though play in the earlier page was complete and valid. A report that a score survived Restart but disappeared on reload is consistent with a write failure.

An imported unfinished snapshot remains usable under the same conditions. The snapshot text is decoded into game state, then the session handles pause and resume. That path does not require a successful preference write. The accepted board size may be retained only in the current session if the browser refuses the later save.

## No implicit retry service

The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

Corrupt data policy follows the rejection branches in detail. Storage quota notes explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The source only calls `getItem` and `setItem` for `PREFERENCES_KEY`. It has no storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. `PreferenceStore` exposes only those two methods. The storage unit test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. Storage testing guide extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# ADR 058: Give additional stored data a distinct namespace

This record explains the naming rule for new stored data while preserving the existing preferences key.

## Context

The first storage decision used a game prefix, a data-family segment and a version suffix separated by dots. The current preferences key still demonstrates that choice: `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. It contains a selected size and a map of per-size best moves in a versioned JSON value.

Additional stored families need a recognizable naming convention without turning a documentation change into an unnecessary migration of existing preferences. This record supersedes ADR 011. The scope is key naming; it does not add another stored family to the current game or replace snapshot export with automatic progress saving.

## Decision

The namespace distinguishes newly introduced storage from keys that a released game already reads. New stored data uses a key of the form np3:THING, where THING is a lowercase plural noun for what is stored. Keys that already exist keep their names. This lets a reader recognize the new convention while the existing preference reader continues to find its current value.

The distinction is intentionally about whether a key already exists, rather than whether its contents look old. Renaming preferences merely to make the key look consistent would require a migration, conflict handling and evidence that the saved size and records survived. No such migration is implemented in the source.

## What remains unchanged in the implementation

`PREFERENCES_KEY` is the one existing key used by `readPreferences` and `writePreferences`. The stored JSON carries `schemaVersion: 1`, `size` and `bestMoves`. Naming a storage key and validating the value are separate responsibilities. A recognizable namespace cannot establish that JSON is well formed, that a size is supported or that a score is a plausible bounded integer.

The parser treats saved data as unknown, checks supported values and falls back to usable defaults when access or validation fails. Writes are caught so the in-memory game remains playable. The namespace decision does not move those browser effects into pure game functions. Preferences store and Storage failure policy describe the existing behavior.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

Renaming every key at once would make the storage inspector look uniform, but would create work and risk unrelated to the new naming need. Continuing the original dotted pattern indefinitely would avoid any new convention while leaving this replacement decision without effect. The selected approach separates continuity for existing data from a clear naming choice for additions.

A single giant application value could avoid choosing new keys at all. That would couple unrelated data families to the same read, validation and write path. The current preferences envelope is appropriately small for size and best moves.

## Reading the rule accurately

The namespace marker is not a new board-code prefix, snapshot version or replay version. Those public formats retain their own identifiers. It is also not a claim that the current preferences schema has been upgraded. Confusing these layers would create a format change where only storage-key naming was intended.

The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. Persistence envelope, Format versioning guide and ADR 053 explain the surrounding boundaries.

This preserves the useful local-storage model while making the successor to the old naming decision explicit. Historical context remains in the superseded record; current readers can follow its replacement link here without treating the old pattern as the convention for additional data.

## The current preferences key and value shape

These are the existing declarations. The new naming decision preserves this identifier rather than silently changing where the application reads its preferences.

```ts
export const DEFAULT_SIZE = GRID_SIZES[0];
export const PREFERENCES_KEY = 'neon-pairs.preferences.v1';
export const PREFERENCES_VERSION = 1;
export interface Preferences {
  readonly size: number;
  readonly bestMoves: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}
export interface PreferenceStore {
  getItem(key: string): string | null;
  setItem(key: string, value: string): void;
}
```
# Target size policy

This page records the control target policy and explains the size constraints already present in the interface styles.

Target size is about the area a person can activate, not the size of a glyph drawn inside it. A card's marker is small, but the native button enclosing the whole card is the target. The same distinction applies to a summary's disclosure marker and the much larger summary row.

## Policy and present coverage

The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.

The current styles are useful building blocks, but they are not proof of every dimension for an arbitrary new element. In particular, `.control` declares minimum height without a general minimum width. A new short-label action could be tall enough while still being too narrow. The policy check and the existing class definition therefore answer related but different questions.

This is a control policy, not a claim of complete accessibility conformance. The visuals specification makes the same distinction for its chosen card minimum. Names, keyboard operation, contrast, visible focus and error behavior still have their own evidence. Interface review checklist gathers those areas without turning a size measurement into a blanket result.

## Size sources in the current code

| Element | Source | Existing size behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Card button | `board.css`, `card.css` | Grid tracks from 44px to 88px, square aspect ratio |
| Button, select, input, textarea using `.control` | `control.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px |
| Reproduction summary | `reproduction.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 12px 16px |
| Deal action row | `controls.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |
| Reproduction action row | `reproduction.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |

`game.css` applies `box-sizing: border-box` globally. The declared height constraints therefore include padding and border. Looking only at text line height would underestimate the target, while adding padding to the measured border box would overestimate it.

Cards have `width: 100%`, `aspect-ratio: 1`, zero padding and a `2px` border. Their width comes from the grid track. They do not establish their minimum using the SVG's coordinates or intrinsic artwork size. The current artwork can change shape while the card target remains the same square.

## Why large boards scroll

The inner board calculates a minimum content width from side length, `--card-min` and `--card-gap`. On a sixteen-column board that is 794px before viewport padding and border. A phone cannot display that whole width at once while keeping the current card minimum.

The implementation chooses an internal scroll area. Its `overflow: auto` and `max-width: 100%` allow the board to extend inside a bounded viewport. The outer page stays within the window. This is the reason a sixteen-column board does not respond like a shrunken thumbnail of a four-column board.

A target-size review can therefore encounter two valid observations at once: every card has its intended dimensions, and some cards are outside the current visible portion of the board. Reachability is supplied by scrolling and keyboard movement. Pointer and touch explains the touch path to the last card; Board keyboard navigation explains arrow access.

A partially clipped card also has a full underlying button box. Clicking the visible part can activate it, after which the current implementation scrolls it fully into view. That behavior does not mean the clipping itself should be measured as the card's intended dimensions. It is an overflow case with a separate focus and pointer timing concern.

## Phone layout affects widths

At `max-width: 599px`, the deal size group fills the row and uses space-between alignment. New Game and Restart receive `flex: 1`. This gives the actions room without hard-coding two button widths. The text and browser control still contribute their intrinsic size constraints.

The reproduction action rows also wrap, with buttons growing on the phone breakpoint. The Board code input has `flex: 1`, a preferred width of `16ch` and `min-width: 0`. The textarea fills its parent and can resize vertically. These choices keep the text tools within the available width rather than making the outer page horizontally scroll.

A visual review at a wide desktop window can miss the consequences of a new wrapper or label. Selectors such as `.controls > button` and `.control-row > button` apply to direct children. If a wrapper changes which element grows, measuring the wrapper rather than the actual button can hide a target-width problem.

The overall content has `16px` page padding and a maximum width of `1120px`. A viewport width is therefore not the same thing as a control's available row width. Panel padding, gaps and borders consume space too. Reading the size policy as a viewport measurement alone would skip the layout where the target actually lives.

## Visible content versus activation area

A native button may contain text, a shape or multiple SVG pieces. In Card, the face SVG and matched check mark are descendants of one button, and the click callback is attached to that button. Their separate geometry does not produce separate tiny controls.

The neutral back is a `12px` span with a rotated border and `aria-hidden="true"`. It is deliberately smaller than the card. Counting its bounds as the input target would describe the drawing rather than the event-handling element. Similarly, the matched check is a state mark, not a separate action with its own click listener.

Focus outlines sit outside the control border and do not add activation area. Hover border changes likewise do not expand the target. Measurements used to assess the policy concern the actual element box; measurements used to assess focus visibility include outline width and offset. The project already has separate helpers for that distinction in `tests/focus-bounds.ts`.

The reproduction summary is another useful case. Its text and disclosure marker occupy only part of a padded native summary element. The element supplies the disclosure interaction. Replacing it with a visually similar small icon could change both target size and semantics; the current source does neither.

## Zoom, density and CSS units

The policy uses CSS pixels. Device pixel ratio affects the mapping to physical pixels, not the DOM geometry reported by `getBoundingClientRect`. A test at device scale 2 can still report a 44px CSS box. Multiplying the bounding-box result by device scale would answer a different question.

The repository's equivalent zoom layout uses a `640x400` viewport with device scale 2. It checks that controls, statistics and the completion summary remain readable and that both small and large boards remain playable. This is useful complementary evidence for a layout that wraps and scrolls rather than simply shrinking every element.

The game does not disable pinch zoom. Card touch handling uses `touch-action: manipulation`, and index.html does not impose a maximum scale. A target remains part of a browser page whose visible scale can change. Zoom behaviour covers the visual contract in more detail.

## Existing evidence and what it establishes

`tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks the default board and control dimensions at `320x640`. It measures `.controls button`, `.controls select` and `.card` boxes and checks minimum width and height. The same file checks large boards at phone and desktop viewports, where the card floor, viewport height and complete focus ring are important.

Those checks establish the existing tested elements at their stated layouts. They do not automatically cover a future control merely because it shares a color or appears next to a tested button. The source selectors and actual bounding box identify the scope of evidence.

For a new feature review, a concise measurement record can identify the viewport, the control's role and name, its width and height and whether it is fully reachable. The record is most useful alongside the rendered layout, because it can reveal that a formally large button is covered by another element or forced beyond the page edge. This is observation of the target in context, not a second numerical policy.

The current game makes many of these checks straightforward by keeping interaction on native DOM elements. There is no canvas hit-map to reconcile with a drawn target. Native controls guide explains that architectural advantage, while Contrast audit and Focus policy cover other properties that a dimension alone cannot establish.
# Motion policy
This page describes the motion currently used by Neon Pairs, its reduced-motion behavior, and the source and tests behind it.

The game has two authored motion effects: a card border transition and a completion pulse. Neither moves a card, changes its dimensions, or delays a game-state update. The relevant declarations live with their components in `src/game/board/card.css` and `src/game/status/status.css`. The broader visual specification is Visuals; turn timing belongs in Turn resolution.

## Card borders

The `.card` rule declares `transition: border-color 120ms ease`. On hover, `.card:hover` changes the border to `var(--text)`. A matched card instead uses `var(--green)`. The transition is limited to the border color: background, outline, size, opacity and SVG geometry have no transition in this rule.

This distinction matters when reading a recording. A reveal replaces the back with the face and changes the card background immediately. The border can still be between colors if the pointer has just entered or left the card. A screenshot taken during that interval does not show the final border value. In `tests/art.e2e.test.ts`, the comparison helper waits for the card's animations to finish before collecting computed styles for this reason.

There is no flip animation. `Card.tsx` conditionally renders either the neutral back span or the `Face` component. The face is absent while the card is closed. Adding a visual flip would therefore be more than a cosmetic adjustment to an existing transform: it would introduce an effect where the current renderer has none. The present markup and identity boundary are described in Card artwork.

Hover also has no gameplay effect. `tests/style.e2e.test.ts` records all computed properties before and after hover, checks that only border-color properties differ, and compares exported game progress. That test is useful when an apparently small visual edit adds a shadow, scale transform or other hover change. Such a difference would depart from the existing V16 behavior even if the card still looked recognizable.

## Reduced motion

Both component stylesheets contain a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query. The card query sets `transition: none`; the status query sets `animation: none` on `.celebrate`. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, new elements run no animation and no transition. This keeps the static visual states available immediately when the preference is active. The existing cards still change their border and artwork when their state changes; the change simply has no interpolated border effect.

The current implementation uses CSS media queries rather than a stored game preference or a React branch. `Card.tsx` does not need to know the preference, and the session does not select an alternative board. The same matched mark, face and victory text appear in both modes. The media query affects presentation rather than game state.

A useful review includes setting the preference before the page loads and completing a board in that mode. `tests/motion.e2e.test.ts` does this through browser media emulation, then checks the banner's computed animation name and a card's transition duration. Those assertions check the existing effects directly. They do not infer reduced-motion support from a screenshot that happens to have been taken after an animation finished.

Changing the preference while the page is open is also a useful manual observation because the implementation is a live CSS media query. There is no application restart step in the code. This is an observation of how the declarations are applied, rather than a separate game lifecycle. It should not be confused with restarting a deal.

## The completion pulse

`GameStatus.tsx` renders the completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. Its class is `victory`, with `celebrate` appended only when the `celebration` prop is true. In `status.css`, `.celebrate` declares `animation: victory-pulse 600ms ease-out 1`.

The keyframes specify a midpoint only. At 50%, the paragraph background is `var(--panel)` and opacity is `0.75`; the start and end come from its underlying styles. There is no `animation-fill-mode` that preserves the midpoint appearance. After the one iteration, the banner remains present in its normal static styling. Its border, padding and text are not removed when the animation finishes.

This is a pulse of the paragraph as a whole, so the opacity also affects its text and border during the effect. It is not a highlight painted behind otherwise opaque text. Contrast audit separates opaque token ratios from a composited estimate for this midpoint. That distinction is helpful when evaluating a captured frame halfway through completion.

The effect neither loops nor emits particles. V18 describes one pulse, a static reduced-motion result, and the absence of flashing and confetti. There are no pulse keyframes on individual cards. A finished board continues to show its matched artwork at full card opacity, as specified in V15.

## Where the celebration flag comes from

The boolean is session data, not a CSS guess based on how many green borders appear. `initialSession` initializes `celebration` to false. `activateSession` sets it from the result of `isWon(game)` after an effective activation that resolves a turn. `replaceGame` clears it when the session changes deals or loads a snapshot.

A completed snapshot can consequently display the completion paragraph with no `celebrate` class. The board is complete, but that load is not a fresh completion event. An unfinished import can later finish through play and receive the normal completion effect. These cases are particularly useful when checking whether an edit has accidentally tied animation to every render of a completed state.

The flag can remain true after the CSS animation has finished. That does not make the effect repeat on every timer update: an existing element retaining the same animation class is different from mounting a new element or changing its animation name. The final game also stops advancing its active elapsed time. The relevant session behavior is covered more fully in Session module.

## Scrolling is separate

The board's scrolling code uses nearest alignment. `Board.tsx` calls `scrollIntoView` after a click, and the focus hook uses the same alignment for keyboard focus. Neither call specifies smooth behavior. The source CSS has no `scroll-behavior: smooth` declaration. Ordinary touch inertia belongs to the browser and is not the authored completion pulse or border transition.

A card can move on screen because its scroll container moves. That movement does not mean the card has a transform animation. This distinction helps reproduce reports about cards near the edge of a large board: the important evidence is the scroll position, focus state and press timing. See Large-board rendering and Focus policy.

The pointer path also deliberately postpones its own scroll adjustment until the click handler runs. Moving a partly clipped card during pointer focus could shift the release target and lose the click. A motion review that only activates fully visible cards misses this interaction. The existing pointer tests include clipped-edge presses and touch taps at the phone, desktop and equivalent zoom layouts.

## Evidence and limits

The normal-motion test checks a `0.12` second card transition whose property list contains only `border-color`. After finishing a board, it checks a `0.6` second banner animation with one iteration. The reduced-motion test checks `animationName === 'none'` on the banner and a parsed card transition duration of zero. These are source-level and computed-style checks.

For a visual change, the existing evidence is strongest when the computed checks and a completion journey agree. A class accidentally applied to the wrong element can produce a plausible screenshot while changing the actual animated surface. Conversely, a screenshot made after 600ms can look static even when an unintended repeated animation is present elsewhere. Reading the declaration and observing the transition answer different questions.

No motion duration here controls whether two cards match or when a mismatch closes. Those decisions come from the game rules and active time. The presentation stays synchronized by rendering their result, rather than waiting for a CSS event to authorize the next action. That separation is the main maintenance benefit of the small current motion surface.
