# Architecture
Architecture is the code structure for Neon Pairs that keeps game rules separate from browser effects.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card activation changes game data first. React renders that data, then the session adapter handles time and saved preferences. The same rules run in browser tests and replay without a browser.

## Game core

- A01 - Keep deck generation, card transitions, logical time, snapshot validation and replay as pure functions under `src/game`. They receive their inputs directly. They don't read the DOM, storage, external random sources or browser clocks.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the reproducibility formats.

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `createGame(boardCode)` | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)` | State after one card activation |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances |
| `isWon(state)` | Whether every position is matched |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)` | Version 1 snapshot JSON |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |
| `replayGame(text)` | Final replay state or `null` |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep active game progress in memory until you export or import a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10.

## Components

- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes status, the board, game controls and reproduction controls. Keep board navigation in `src/game/board`, controls in `src/game/controls` and session behavior in `src/game/session`. Keep each component's props and styles beside it.

- A08 - A card mounts its face SVG only while revealed or matched. Hidden card identity stays out of DOM attributes, accessible names and diagnostic globals. Tests can know a deck from its documented board code. The app gives them no solver endpoint.

- A09 - Use native browser input and the shared card activation function. Keep focus position in the board component. Focus movement changes presentation, never the deck or move count. Input defines the keys and focus rules.

## Evidence

- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.

- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.

## Changes

- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

The game specification defines the behavior this structure implements.
# Technology
Technology is the build and language specification for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

The game runs offline from one HTML file. Browser controls and inline SVG provide the board, input and artwork.

## Stack

- T01 - Use React with TypeScript and DOM rendering. Use native buttons, a native select and CSS Grid. Use no component library.

- T02 - Pin these packages and keep the lockfile. The stable versions were checked on 31 October 2026:

| Package | Version | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `react`, `react-dom` | `19.3.1` | Browser UI |
| `typescript` | `7.0.2` | Type checking |
| `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom` | `19.3.0` | React types |
| `vite` | `8.3.5` | Build |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `6.1.2` | React build integration |
| `vite-plugin-singlefile` | `2.3.4` | One HTML distribution |
| `vitest` | `5.0.5` | Unit tests |
| `@playwright/test` | `1.64.1` | Browser tests |
| `@types/node` | `24.19.2` | Build and test types |

TypeScript 7 is a stable release, as the [release announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) describes. The [React versions page](https://react.dev/versions) lists the stable React release family.

## Language

- T03 - Use Node.js 24.19 or later and npm. Keep browser and Node compiler projects separate. Use ESM, static imports and type-only imports for types.

Use Node `26.12.1`, npm `11.20.0` and Playwright `1.64.1` with Chromium `156.0.8078.4` as the named compatibility combination. Record the locked install, build, unit tests and browser journeys with those exact versions in the project README before calling the combination tested. Other supported versions need their own results.

- T04 - Enable TypeScript strictness, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Keep type checking separate from bundling. Vite's [TypeScript support](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#typescript) transpiles code without checking types.

- T05 - Model project data with exact types and validate unknown data where it enters the game. Use narrowing instead of `any`, suppressed diagnostics or unchecked casts. Derive state unions from their named values.

- T06 - Keep behavior and its code, styles and tests together. Aim for 100 lines per TypeScript file and keep authored TypeScript files at or below 200 lines. Split by behavior when a file grows. Use direct imports from the file that defines a behavior.

## Commands

- T07 - Provide these commands:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm ci` | Install the locked dependencies |
| `npm run dev` | Serve the game locally |
| `npm run typecheck` | Check every compiler project |
| `npm test` | Run unit tests for the game rules |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Build from current source, then run browser checks in fresh contexts against that build |
| `npm run build` | Type check and emit `dist/index.html` |
| `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` | Read replay JSON with the output and exit behavior in C14 |

The browser command must fail if its build fails. It must never fall back to an earlier `dist`. Stop development servers and watchers you start before finishing the work.

## Distribution

- T08 - `dist/index.html` contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play. It opens directly from disk without another file or a network request. Use the system font. Keep browser zoom enabled.

- T09 - Serve the game from a local HTTP origin when checking saved preferences. Storage on a `file:` URL differs between browsers, as the [localStorage documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage) explains. If storage is unavailable, play continues for the current session.

- T10 - Keep dependencies in development and build tooling where possible. The game uses no service, account, external asset, analytics or API key. Dependency installation can use the network. Playing the distribution doesn't use it.

The game specification connects this stack to the other requirements.
# Test policy

This page explains the verification layers used by Neon Pairs and the kinds of failures each layer can establish.

The repository checks rule transitions, serialized input, source conventions and complete browser journeys. These checks share documented examples but do not all run in the same environment. `npm test` runs Vitest; `npm run test:e2e` builds the current application and diagnostic entries, then uses Node's test runner with Playwright browser support.

## Focused evidence stays near behavior

The core has adjacent tests such as `game.test.ts`, `deck.test.ts`, `snapshot.test.ts` and `replay.test.ts`. Their names make the behavior under discussion easy to locate before reading the whole suite. A feature's rules.ts has a rules.test.ts beside it. Complete interaction journeys remain at the application test level, where focus, storage, browser lifecycle and delivery can be observed together.

Adjacency is useful because a transition and its evidence can be read in one pass. It does not mean every production file in the repository has a one-to-one test file. Some concerns have several focused files: completion, move limits, snapshot selection and replay ordering each get separate attention. Other helpers are exercised through a broader behavior or browser journey.

The architecture specification A10 asks for focused tests near behavior, independent literal generation vectors, transitions checked against stated rules and built HTML checked from disk as well as served. Those are different obligations because no single test environment can establish all of them.

## What Vitest includes

`vitest.config.ts` includes `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. It does not include the browser files in `tests`, which end in `.e2e.test.ts` and run under the separate command. There is no hidden browser suite behind `npm test`.

Most unit tests use `node:assert/strict` with `test` imported from Vitest. They call pure functions directly. Clock arithmetic receives numerical observations; session transitions receive a session object; preference tests pass a memory or failing store. This makes failures specific: a mismatch boundary can be checked without waiting for a real timeout.

The script tests also run here. `replay.test.ts` launches child processes to exercise command output and failure exits, and the source-audit files read authored files and configuration. The CLI test has a 60-second timeout because child processes can be slow on a busy verifier. That allowance is test scheduling, not a game timing constant.

## Independence for generated data

A generator test that computes its expected deck using the same generator can prove little about compatibility. The repository instead contains a literal example deck for `np1-4-1`, initial recurrence values and independent rejection vectors. Browser support also has `specDeal` in `tests/deal-oracle.ts`, which expresses the shuffle with BigInt arithmetic.

The rejection tests cover both a draw above the accepted limit and a draw exactly at it. That equality case matters because a one-character comparison change would alter the seeded result. Completion tests iterate supported grid sizes and activate every actual pair to prove that each generated board can finish with one move per pair.

The literal fixture and oracle serve different purposes. A literal fixes a public example. An independent implementation can check more combinations but can still share a mistaken interpretation of the written rule. The documented format, literal vectors and independent arithmetic together provide stronger evidence than any one of them alone.

## State transitions and identity

`activateCard` returns the same state object for ignored input: an invalid index, a matched position, the already revealed first card or input during a mismatch. Tests can check both the unchanged values and reference identity. Identity matters because the session controller and memoized presentation use it to avoid unnecessary work.

A successful first activation changes `started` and selection without adding a move. A second distinct activation adds one move and either matches immediately or opens a mismatch. The rule tests can check this without going through pointer events. Browser journeys then establish that actual buttons call that same path.

The cap tests cover continued matching and victory at `MOVES_MAX = 999_999`, and elapsed-time tests cover the total cap. A limit on the number displayed or serialized is not evidence that play should terminate there. The meaningful regression is whether ordinary transitions still work at the boundary.

## Format validation evidence

Snapshot tests check outer keys, numeric bounds, matched-position consistency and each selection form. `snapshot-selection.test.ts` focuses on nested selection invariants. A selected index must name an available position, a mismatch must involve different faces and complete matched pairs must be represented together. The decoder reconstructs its deck from the code before checking these relationships.

Replay tests add ordering and action count constraints. Equal timestamps preserve array order, while logical time advances before each activation. `replay-order.test.ts` checks a same-time third activation blocked by the preceding mismatch. These are rules about accepted actions, not browser task order.

Round trips establish that the serializer and decoder agree on valid states, but rejection cases are necessary because both could otherwise agree on an overly permissive format. The repository's exact-key helpers and validators make those cases inspectable. Snapshot format and Replay format provide the product-facing definitions.

## Browser command and fresh output

The end-to-end script is:

```sh
npm run build && npm run build:art && node --test --test-concurrency=1 "tests/*.e2e.test.ts"
```

The production build type checks first. Both build stages precede the test runner with `&&`, so a failure prevents the suite from opening an older output. `build:art` creates the face sheet and the session harness separately from `dist/index.html`.

The browser wrapper in `tests/browser-test.ts` creates a new context per journey and registers its closure with the Node test context. It collects page errors and asserts that none occurred after a successful journey body. It creates an artifact directory from the test name and restricts output paths to a filename. A shared browser and local server are closed in the file-level teardown.

The standard journey timeout is 30 seconds and the long one is 90 seconds. Playwright assertions use a 15-second configured timeout. These values make verification tolerant of busy machines; they do not lengthen the logical mismatch interval, which controlled-clock tests exercise precisely.

## Disk and HTTP evidence

`tests/game-fixture.ts` defines a `file:` URL for the distribution and separate URLs for the two diagnostic builds. `tests/artifact-server.ts` also serves the built HTML on an ephemeral loopback port, accepting only `/`. This is a test server around the finished file, not the Vite development server.

Disk delivery demonstrates that the HTML carries its own code and assets. HTTP-origin journeys establish preference persistence in a browser environment with a stable storage origin for the journey. A result from one mode does not establish the other, because storage behavior on local files varies.

`build-output.e2e.test.ts` reads the HTML and checks for the excluded fetch and module-preload markers. Browser journeys can additionally watch requests. Source inspection, artifact inspection and actual browser behavior contribute different evidence about offline delivery. Offline delivery explains why all three are useful.

## Browser interactions that pure tests cannot see

Arrow navigation tests can check the helper's target arithmetic directly, but only the browser can show where focus lands, whether Tab leaves and whether scrolling keeps the focus ring visible. Native click behavior also matters for keyboard activation, context menus and touch scrolling. The card component uses the native click path rather than a separate game action per input method.

Artwork tests render all 128 faces through the real `Card` component in the separate face sheet. Layout journeys cover large boards, visible scrollbars, zoom and touch. Accessibility journeys inspect the Chromium accessibility tree through a complete keyboard interaction. The README explicitly separates this tree evidence from a spoken screen-reader acceptance journey.

These distinctions prevent overclaiming. A passing tree check does not mean a human has listened to every announcement. A passing layout measurement does not mean every browser family has been tested. Browser support and Accessibility audit are the related places for that evidence.

## Time and lifecycle regressions

The clock tests are intentionally layered. `browser-clock.test.ts` checks arithmetic, while `session.test.ts` checks stale generations and paused state. Browser files exercise hidden intervals, idle pause periods, fractional observations and exports between timer callbacks.

`fractional-clock.e2e.test.ts` overrides the observed clock and sends an overdue click in the same browser task. No scheduled timer can run first, so this isolates the controller's synchronize-before-activate behavior. `idle-clock.e2e.test.ts` avoids inspecting the game repeatedly during inactivity, exposing bugs that an incidental export synchronization could otherwise mask.

The session harness makes teardown observable by unmounting the actual game. `timer-lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` instruments timers and visibility listeners, checks that one active timer exists, then checks cleanup after unmount. It also follows an earlier mismatch with a later mismatch in the same deal. This catches mistakes that merely changing the deal generation would not expose.

## Source and runtime records

Source audit notes records the package, compiler, source and naming patterns inspected by the static checks. Browser setup separately writes its observed runtime versions and can enforce the named combination. These records describe different evidence; neither replaces a behavior test.

For a review, the useful account names the changed behavior and the check that observes it. Code review guide gives examples of that mapping.

# Browser test guide
This guide explains the Node and Playwright harness used to exercise Neon Pairs through its built browser interface.

The suite opens generated HTML, not the Vite development page. It uses Node's test runner and Playwright's browser automation library. That combination explains several otherwise surprising details: tests import a local `test` wrapper, the package command controls file concurrency, and browser assertions have a locally configured timeout. Start with Test strategy for the reason each layer exists.

## The normal entry point

From a writable project checkout, the complete command is:

```sh
npm run test:e2e
```

In `package.json`, this expands to:

```sh
npm run build && npm run build:art && node --test --test-concurrency=1 "tests/*.e2e.test.ts"
```

`build` performs type checking before Vite emits `dist/index.html`. `build:art` emits `.art/index.html` and `.session/index.html` through separate configurations. A failure in either build stops the command before the test runner. This prevents accidentally testing an older distribution after a failed compile.

The commands write build outputs and browser artifacts, so they need a writable checkout with the reviewed JSON expectation files consumed by the tests; see Known issues. The README records a successful run.

During focused development, invoking Node for one browser file can shorten diagnosis after a current build exists. Such an invocation does not perform the build chain by itself and does not replace the full release command. A failure that disappears only when old output is used remains a failure of the source being reviewed.

## What the wrapper owns

`tests/browser-test.ts` imports `before`, `after` and `test` from `node:test`. Its file-level setup creates `.browser-work` and `test-results`, sets `TEMP` and `TMP` for browser work, obtains version information and launches headless Chromium. It then starts the private artifact server.

The exported `test` accepts a name, an async body, optional browser-context options, a scrollbar mode and a timeout. The body receives `browser`, `context`, `page` and `gameURL`, plus an artifact helper. Each case gets a new context and page. The context is registered for cleanup with the Node test context. The wrapper also collects uncaught page errors and expects the collection to be empty after the body completes.

A failed assertion can end the body before that final page-error assertion, so the final check is not a universal crash report. Browser automation errors and page errors are different sources of failure. Looking at the first meaningful failure usually gives a better diagnosis than reading only the trailing timeout.

The `after` hook closes the normal browser, any lazily created visible-scrollbar browser, and the server. Tests creating an extra context themselves close it explicitly, as the phone completion journey does in a `finally` block. This is practical resource ownership, not an assumption that process exit will always clean up successfully.

## Disk and HTTP URLs answer different questions

`GAME_URL` in `tests/game-fixture.ts` is a file URL for `dist/index.html`. `ART_URL` and `SESSION_URL` similarly address diagnostic builds. Disk loading is the delivery path: the game should remain playable without sibling assets or network requests.

`gameURL`, supplied by the wrapper, is the HTTP origin from `serveArtifact`. The server reads the emitted HTML, listens on `127.0.0.1` using an available port, serves `/`, and returns 404 for other paths. It does not serve source, fixture JSON or a diagnostic API. Saved-preference tests use this stable origin within their context so reload can observe the same local storage.

A persistence test that uses the disk URL can become dependent on browser-specific storage treatment. A delivery test that uses only HTTP can miss a file-loading problem. Existing tests deliberately use both paths. Browser support describes the resulting compatibility claims; Storage testing covers the persistence contract in more depth.

## Load a deterministic deal through the controls

`loadFixedBoard(page, url)` navigates, opens the native reproduction disclosure, fills Board code with `np1-4-1`, selects Load board, closes the disclosure and expects 16 cards. Its default URL is the built disk file. Tests that need HTTP pass the wrapper's `gameURL` explicitly.

The helper does not expose the application's state. Its pair positions come from `src/game/game.fixture.ts`, whose literal deck matches the published format example. This supports complete games while keeping hidden cards anonymous to the DOM. `play.e2e.test.ts` checks that closed cards have no SVG face and that diagnostic face attributes are absent before solving.

A compact behavior case follows the existing style:

```ts
import { expect, test } from './browser-test.ts';
import { loadFixedBoard, moves } from './game-fixture.ts';

test('a repeated first reveal leaves the move count at zero', async ({ page }) => {
  await loadFixedBoard(page);
  const card = page.locator('.card').nth(2);
  await card.click();
  await card.click();
  await expect(page.locator('.card.revealed')).toHaveCount(1);
  expect(await moves(page)).toBe(0);
});
```

The example uses the known deal, a native user action and observations available in the interface. The expected result does not call the implementation being tested.

## Selectors follow the observation

Control actions generally use accessible roles or labels with exact names. The size control is a combobox. Board code is a labeled input. Snapshot JSON is a labeled textarea. The disclosure uses a native summary element. These selectors exercise the same discoverability that a keyboard or assistive-software user needs.

`.card` and state classes are useful when inspecting card counts, position order and geometry. A positional locator is appropriate because the format defines row-order indices. It should not become a way to discover hidden identities. Card identity expectations come from the deterministic input, not an undocumented browser global.

Shared label constants keep ordinary journeys readable, but literal contract cases protect the actual wording. Changing a control's constant can otherwise change the test lookup and production label together. The dedicated contract files are deliberate independent evidence, rather than duplicate stylistic preferences.

## Time is a controlled input

`loadTimedBoard` installs Playwright's clock before navigation, loads the fixed deal and pauses at a later clock value. Time-sensitive journeys then use `page.clock.runFor` for exact active intervals. One test opens a miss, advances 200ms, hides the page, advances 2000ms while hidden, returns and checks the remaining 599ms plus 1ms boundary.

Headless Chromium keeps its tabs visible in this environment. The visibility tests therefore override `document.hidden` and dispatch `visibilitychange`, exercising the adapter input the game actually reads. Opening another tab is not a reliable substitute for this setup.

The fractional-clock file uses a narrower instrument: an init script replaces `performance.now` and a test-only event changes its reading. It can advance time and issue a click in the same browser task. That reproduces an overdue mismatch even if the scheduled callback has not run. The test proves synchronization before activation rather than measuring how quickly a timer fires on the host.

`exportedSnapshot` uses the visible export control and parses its textarea. Export synchronizes active time, so it can observe more than the most recent status render. This is useful for clock evidence, but it can also hide an idle-return bug if called during every wait. The idle-clock cases deliberately make no intermediate reads while hidden or paused. See Flaky-test notes for the distinction.

## Focus needs a real journey

Calling `.focus()` is useful to establish a starting position. It does not prove that Tab can enter the board naturally. The keyboard and accessibility journeys include real Tab, Shift+Tab, arrow, Enter and Space events. Edge assertions check that arrows stop rather than wrap; Tab exit checks that the board does not trap focus.

The `moveKeyboardTo` helper reads only the currently focused card, computes row and column deltas and presses one arrow per step. It neither activates the destination nor reads its face. Matched cards remain reachable, and their disabled action state is checked separately from their focusability.

`focus-bounds.ts` measures card rectangles against the board viewport and window. It includes outline width and outline offset, along with viewport client borders, so a visible card with a clipped ring does not pass as fully visible. The quarter-pixel comparison allowance handles geometry rounding. It does not weaken card target-size assertions.

The pointer-focus cases deliberately click a sliver of a card near the board edge. They use mouse coordinates or touchscreen taps after arranging scroll position. A locator click that automatically scrolls the target fully into view would erase the condition under test. Wheel cases wait for changing scroll position and then a sequence of stable frames before clicking.

## Layout modes and diagnostic entries

Context options configure viewport, device scale and touch emulation. Visible-scrollbar mode removes Chromium's default `--hide-scrollbars` argument; its tests establish that scrollbars occupy space before inspecting the board. Browser support lists the actual configurations.

The face sheet and unmount harness are separate builds, with their own disk URLs. They keep diagnostic controls out of the game distribution. Fixtures guide explains how those entries support artwork and lifecycle observations.

## Artifacts and runtime records

The wrapper turns a test name into an alphanumeric-and-hyphen directory under `test-results`. `artifacts.outputPath` accepts a basename and rejects a path containing directories. Existing cases write face-sheet PNGs and an accessibility journey JSON file through this helper.

The runtime record is `test-results/browser-runtime.json`. It contains Node, npm, Playwright and Chromium versions, plus whether named-combination enforcement was requested. `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION=1` adds an exact comparison to the named tool set. `PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE` selects an alternate executable, but the recorded browser version still determines what was actually tested.

There is no automatic trace or screenshot-on-every-failure configuration in this wrapper. The presence of a screenshot from another case does not prove the failed case captured its final state. Artifact names and content are evidence created by their specific tests. Accessibility audit describes the normalized tree artifact and its limits.

For a release, use the complete build-and-run command and interpret failures with their environment and fixture availability. For a local diagnosis, preserve the failing action order and control only the browser input needed to reproduce it. Those two habits keep a fast test useful without turning an incomplete run into a compatibility claim.
# Form layout guide

This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls.

The game has two kinds of control groups: the always-visible deal bar and the text tools inside Reproduce a game. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ. This guide describes those differences so a markup refactor can preserve the actual interaction rather than just one screenshot.

## A map of the current groups

| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Two buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. Native controls guide explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

The labels come from `control-labels.ts`. Keeping visible text in those constants does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the imported value and the actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.

At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches its children. The size group takes the full line and distributes its label and select with space-between alignment. The direct child buttons grow equally. The DOM order stays Grid size, New Game, Restart while the layout moves into two lines.

That stability matters for keyboard order. The CSS changes wrapping, not the tab sequence or source order. A visual rearrangement implemented by moving DOM nodes could affect where Tab goes; the present media query does not need to do that.

The group is not a native form. Changing the select calls the controller immediately. There is no Apply button or submission that combines the selected size with one of the deal actions. Control bar documents those callbacks and what they replace.

## Board-code form: one label, one submission

BoardCodeForm renders a grid form with a `6px` gap. Its first child is the label. The next is `.control-row`, a wrapping flex container with a `12px` gap and bottom alignment. Inside are the input and the Load board submit button.

The input has `flex: 1` and `width: 16ch`. The preferred width reflects code-like text, while flex growth gives it available space. The shared control stylesheet sets `min-width: 0` for inputs and textareas so their intrinsic width does not force the page wider than its container.

The button is the form's explicit submit action. Its ref supports successful keyboard submission when the input is replaced. The form prevents normal page navigation, reads `boardCode` and calls the loader. The label stays outside the row so a wrapped button does not detach it from the field's visual group.

On the phone breakpoint, direct child buttons of `.control-row` get `flex: 1`. This selector is shared with the snapshot action row. A wrapper inserted between the row and a button would change this rule's target; a DOM cleanup can therefore have a mobile layout consequence even when desktop placement looks unchanged.

## Snapshot field: a larger editing surface

Reproduction's body is a grid with a `12px` gap and `4px 16px 16px` padding. The Snapshot JSON label and textarea are adjacent children of this grid. The textarea uses five rows, fills its available width and can resize vertically.

Export replaces its value with readable JSON. Import reads the current value. There is no automatic serialization on every game render, so the field can hold a draft while the player inspects cards or changes a deal. Its controlled state is independent of the board-code input's generation-keyed default value.

The two snapshot buttons follow in a `.control-row`. Both are `type="button"`, which makes the action semantics explicit even if the surrounding layout later changes. The current component does not depend on a textarea Enter press to decide which snapshot action to perform.

A manual copy workflow uses native text selection. The card-specific `user-select: none` rule does not apply to this field. Vertical resize and long structured text can make the disclosure tall, but the field remains an ordinary part of document flow.

## Shared control styling

`.control` sets minimum height, padding, border, radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. It is imported by both Controls and the reproduction components. The selectors for button and select add a pointer cursor, while the input and textarea selector handles shrinking.

The shared class does not create a universal component with all semantics and validation built in. A select still has native options, an input still has its own maximum length, and a textarea still has multiline editing. Their association, callbacks and error descriptions remain in the JSX.

`game.css` sets global border-box sizing and a system sans-serif font at `16px` with a `24px` line height. Form controls inherit the font instead of taking a separate browser default. The focus outline is shared through `:focus-visible`, so a form layout also needs enough space for that outline to be seen.

## Outcome text is outside the disclosure

The load notice paragraph and Resume are in `.load-status`, following details rather than living inside `.reproduction-body`. The row has a `12px` gap, wraps and reserves at least `56px` of height. The paragraph grows and has `min-width: 0`.

This placement makes a paused-load outcome usable after the disclosure closes. It also means a selector that searches only inside details will not find Resume or the notice. Tests deliberately inspect the adjacent load-status location. Error display guide follows its content and the load buttons' `aria-describedby` relationships.

Turn output is elsewhere, near the board instructions. The layout does not put every changing sentence inside the form body. The distinction is useful when testing a large phone board: result visibility near the board and load feedback near the text tools are separate observations.

## Reflow and review examples

At a narrow width, the page should be read as a vertical flow of labeled groups rather than a fixed matrix of coordinates. The existing wrapped rows and shrinking fields let content determine height. The default board fits the narrow layout, while a large board confines its own overflow to its viewport.

A longer draft can remain in an input even when not all of its characters are visible at once; native text editing can scroll within the field. That is different from making the whole outer page wider. A multiline snapshot can expand or scroll internally without turning its label into a floating overlay.

The equivalent zoom test at `640x400`, device scale 2, checks readable controls, statistics and completion output. It also uses the snapshot tools at that constrained layout. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` verifies labels, native limits and selectable export text. Together the sources cover geometry and editing behavior without defining a new generic form framework.

For a proposed name field, these label and native-control patterns are relevant background, but there is no implemented name form to copy. Text entry policy, Name length policy and Duplicate names policy own its separate acceptance rules. The current interface has no name-field placeholder, character counter, error precedence or field order.
# Error display guide

This page explains how failed board-code and snapshot loads are reported without replacing the current game.

The current UI has two validation outcomes that are errors: `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. They describe the attempted load, not a broken game. The player can correct the draft and retry while the current deal remains available.

## The visible location

Reproduction renders a paragraph with `id="load-notice"` and class `load-notice` inside `.load-status`. That container follows the native details element. It is adjacent to the reproduction tools but outside their collapsible body.

Both Load board and Load snapshot carry `aria-describedby="load-notice"`. Their visible names remain the action labels; the description associates the nearby outcome with those actions. The field labels stay Board code and Snapshot JSON rather than being replaced with an error sentence.

Because the paragraph is outside details, it remains in document flow when the panel is closed. A person does not have to reopen the JSON field merely to see the most recent load notice or Resume. The `.load-status` flex row wraps, has a `12px` gap and a `56px` minimum height; its paragraph can grow and shrink within the available width.

The same load outcome is also published through the game's feedback path. Announcements policy describes that event handling. The local paragraph's role here is visible context beside the load tools, not a second independent validation system.

## Who decides that a load failed

BoardCodeForm reads its draft through FormData and calls the `loadBoard` prop. The controller in `use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace and checks `parseBoardCode`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidBoard)` and returns false before clock reset or replacement.

Reproduction passes the complete snapshot draft to `loadSnapshot`. The controller calls `decodeSnapshot`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidSnapshot)` and returns false, again before resetting or replacing the game. The textarea component does not try to validate JSON structure itself.

`SessionNotice` in `session.ts` owns the literal messages. The shared `notice` helper sets both `feedback` and `loadNotice` and advances announcement identity. The exact words therefore come from the session boundary that knows the operation failed, rather than being duplicated in each field's change handler.

This ordering is important. If a load reset the timer before parsing, even an invalid draft could alter play. If it replaced the game before reporting failure, the notice would not describe the preservation behavior promised by the controls specification. The current callbacks validate first.

## What a failure preserves

A failed board-code load leaves the input's DOM node intact because generation does not change. Its edited value remains available. A failed snapshot load leaves Reproduction's local string state intact. Neither failure clears the draft to make the panel look clean.

The game object, board size, matched positions, selection, moves and elapsed state are not replaced by the error path. The existing game can continue to advance active time. An invalid input is not an imported pause, and it does not freeze a pending mismatch merely because a notice appeared.

Focus memory also survives because Board is not remounted. A player who last visited a far card can return there after correcting a form. The current saved size is unchanged by a failed load; successful replacement is what updates that preference.

The load notice is a session field separate from the game. Adding it can produce a render without changing card state. This is why comparing the complete session object for identity is different from asserting that gameplay was replaced. Game state model and Session module explain those boundaries.

## Focus depends on how submission began

A click on Load board ordinarily leaves focus on the button. If the code is invalid, BoardCodeForm does not issue another focus call. A keyboard Enter submission from inside Board code leaves focus in the field on failure, so the user can continue editing.

On successful Enter submission, the input is about to be replaced because it is keyed by generation. BoardCodeForm explicitly focuses its Load board ref when the callback returns true. That is a success-path focus correction, not an error-summary jump.

Load snapshot is a `type="button"` action. Its handler passes local text to the controller and does not move focus elsewhere on failure or success. The snapshot textarea stays mounted. Export likewise keeps its action focus and fills the field rather than focusing or selecting it automatically.

These cases show why “errors focus the field” would be an inaccurate description of this interface. The source preserves the user's current interaction where it can. Focus policy covers the complete set of current focus transfers.

## Notices are outcomes, not sticky field annotations

`loadNotice` is one session string used for the latest published load outcome. It is not an error object keyed separately by field. The UI does not render two simultaneous field-specific error paragraphs or an error list above the panel.

After an invalid Board code attempt followed by an invalid snapshot attempt, the visible notice is the snapshot message. The Board code draft can still be invalid; the notice records the most recent action rather than continuously describing all field values.

Editing the snapshot string changes local state but does not itself clear the controller's notice. Editing Board code is native uncontrolled editing and likewise does not call a notice-clearing function. The outcome can remain visible while the user works on a correction.

Export replaces textarea text but does not explicitly clear `loadNotice`. Card turns update feedback without rewriting the load notice. New Game, Restart and a successful board-code replacement clear both through `replaceGame(..., false)`. Successful snapshot loading replaces the notice with its load outcome, and Resume clears it when continuing play.

This lifecycle explains a report that an old load message is still visible after editing. The message is action feedback, not a live validator attached to every keystroke. Adding an on-change clearing behavior would be a change to this lifecycle, not a fix to a missing CSS state.

## Format validity is more than native limits

Board code has a 32-character entry cap, but many shorter strings are invalid. An unsupported size, zero seed, leading zeros or malformed separators fail the parser even when the input is well below its native maximum. The loader's surrounding trim is a deliberate adapter step, not broad syntax repair.

Snapshot JSON has a 65536-character textarea limit and a UTF-8 byte bound in the decoder. Malformed JSON is only one failure kind. Unsupported versions, unknown properties, inconsistent matched positions, invalid selections and out-of-range counters can also produce the same UI error.

The UI intentionally gives the short outcome rather than exposing the decoder's internal reasoning. There is no implemented per-property error report or highlighted JSON line number. Import safety policy and Snapshot format are the useful debugging references for engineers handling a rejected draft.

A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class.

## Existing visual and semantic treatment

The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run.

The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. Form layout guide explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure.

Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in Name length policy and Duplicate names policy. The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component.

## Evidence for preservation and retry

`tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause.

`tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys.

A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning.
# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes deal controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction controls. It calls `useGame` once to obtain the current session and actions.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. Session module explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large board

A 16 by 16 board has 256 cards. Active time can update on the 40ms observation cadence, but most ticks do not change any card's appearance. `advanceGame` retains the deck and matched array and, outside a mismatch change, retains the selection object. `Board` memoizes face-up and matched sets from those references.

`Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Its props are primitive presentation values and stable callbacks. On an elapsed-only update, face, matched, tabIndex, size and handlers stay equal, so the cards do not all need to rerender. The parent can still update the statistic.

A pending mismatch changes selection as its remainder decreases, so the face-up set can be recomputed. The resulting card props can nevertheless remain equal until the selection actually closes. This distinction explains why immutable reference stability is useful even though the board's parent renders more often than its cards.

Memoization is not a substitute for correct state ownership. Mutating the matched array in place could keep its reference stable while changing its meaning, causing derived sets to miss an update. The transition code returns a new matched array when a pair is found, matching the assumptions of the board's memoization.

## Concealed identity is a prop boundary

`Board` knows the immutable deck, but it passes `face={null}` for every position outside the derived face-up set. `Card` then renders only a decorative back. It does not mount `Face` and hide it with CSS. Its accessible description omits face design when the supplied face is null.

When revealed or matched, a card gets the face number and renders inline SVG. `Face` marks the SVG as decorative, while the button's label describes the visible design. The board can therefore hold authoritative identity without exposing concealed identity through every child element.

This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.

## Local focus and DOM work

`useBoardFocus` holds a focused index initialized to zero and refs to the viewport and grid. Arrow handling calls `navigationTarget`; a non-null result prevents the browser default and focuses the target button with `preventScroll: true`. Focus events update the remembered index.

`useNearestScroll` listens to the board viewport's scroll events and remembers the reported position. For keyboard focus it restores that position before calling `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. This accounts for Chromium's automatic centering on focus. A click scrolls after activation so the pressed card is not moved under a held pointer before release.

These browser operations belong with the board presentation, not `GameState`. A replay contains positions and logical times, not a scroll offset. A snapshot can load into a differently sized viewport. Keeping focus and scrolling local preserves that independence.

## Replacement and imperative focus

`Game` gives `Board` a ref typed as `BoardFocus`. The board exposes only `focusRemembered()` through `useImperativeHandle`. The parent does not receive the whole grid DOM or a collection of card nodes.

Resume uses that limited operation, then calls the controller's resume action. A replacement instead increments generation and changes the board key, remounting its local focus state. `BoardCodeForm` keys its uncontrolled input by that same generation, so successful loading replaces the old draft with the current code.

A generation is consequently a lifecycle boundary shared by adapters and components. It is not a reason to put DOM state in the session core. The rule functions remain unaware of keyed mounts, refs or focus methods.

## Effects and cleanup

Browser effects pair setup with cleanup: the clock removes its listener and timeout, and nearest scrolling removes its viewport listener. The separate session harness lets tests unmount the real game and measure that cleanup. Clock design details the active flag, generation checks and scheduling lifetime.

## Keeping a change on the right side

An incorrect pair count starts in the game state and derivation, not in JSX text. An incorrect load-pause state starts in session replacement, not a disabled style. An incorrect arrow stop starts in the numerical navigation helper, while an incorrect scroll alignment starts in the DOM hook. The boundary narrows where an explanation should begin.

The architecture specification permits shared support when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. It does not introduce a generic hooks or utilities layer merely because several files use React. Current direct imports keep ownership legible, and the module policy describes feature placement. Together they make small components useful without making rendering the owner of the game rules.
# Source layout

This page is a map of the current Neon Pairs source tree and the responsibilities of its files.

Paths here are relative to the project root. They describe authored source and configured outputs. Module layout policy explains placement decisions; this page is for finding the implementation.

## Entry and project root

`index.html` contains the document metadata, the `root` element and the development module entry `/src/main.tsx`. It declares English, a responsive viewport, the theme color `#090B14` and the title Neon Pairs. The source HTML references a module; the production HTML is assembled by Vite and the single-file plugin.

`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.

The root also holds `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, four compiler configuration files, three Vite configurations and `vitest.config.ts`. `.prettierrc.json` configures formatting; `.prettierignore` and `.gitignore` identify generated or local work. The README records setup, commands, delivery, replay and the named runtime evidence.

## Game composition

`Game.tsx` calls `useGame`, passes session values and controller actions into the UI, and imports `game.css`. Its output is a single main element containing the heading, instructions, deal controls, statistics, turn feedback, board and reproduction controls.

Its one extra coordination operation is Resume. It asks the board's imperative ref to focus the remembered card, then calls the controller's resume action. That keeps the DOM focus handoff outside the core state. `Board` is keyed by `session.generation`, so a replacement remounts the board's local state.

`game.css` defines root colors and spacing values, system typography, page geometry, global focus styling and the reserved turn-feedback area. The more specific board, control and status rules live beside their components. CSS organization records selectors and cascade relationships.

## Core modules directly under src/game

| File | What a reader finds there |
| --- | --- |
| `deck.ts` | Supported sizes, seed bounds, board-code parser and formatter, seeded shuffle and immutable board description |
| `selection.ts` | The closed, one-card and mismatch discriminated union |
| `game.ts` | `GameState`, caps, creation, victory, face-up positions, activation and logical advancement |
| `elapsed-time.ts` | Display formatting from elapsed milliseconds |
| `saved-format.ts` | Small shared JSON, object, key, integer and byte helpers |
| `snapshot-selection.ts` | Validation of matched positions and nested selection |
| `snapshot.ts` | Snapshot version and bound, serialization and complete-state validation |
| `replay.ts` | Replay limits, structured problems, ordered actions and final state |

These files use ordinary TypeScript functions and data. The core is not a React context or reducer hook. It can be imported by the session adapter and by the replay CLI without mounting the application.

`generateBoard` returns a frozen description with a frozen deck. `GameState` extends that description. Runtime progress is returned as new objects by transitions; ignored actions can return the existing object. This pattern explains why the board's memoized sets can survive clock-only updates.

## Core test files

`game.test.ts` checks card transitions and logical advancement. `completion.test.ts` finishes every supported size. `move-cap.test.ts` exercises play and records at the maximum move count. `elapsed-time.test.ts` covers the formatter and related elapsed behavior.

`deck.test.ts` checks parsing and generation. `deck-rejection.test.ts` references independently generated vectors for rejection-sampling boundaries. `game.fixture.ts` contains the example code, literal deck, pair positions, initial generator states and shared numerical specification vectors.

`snapshot.test.ts` and `snapshot-selection.test.ts` cover the outer state and nested validation. `replay.test.ts` and `replay-order.test.ts` cover replay acceptance and ordering. These files live near the rules even when a narrow regression deserves a different test filename from the principal module.

## Session directory

`session/session.ts` defines `Session`, the import notices and the pure session operations `initialSession`, `replaceGame`, `tickSession` and `activateSession`. It connects a game transition to feedback, completion state and preferences without itself calling the browser.

`session/use-game.ts` is the React controller. It reads initial preferences, creates the initial fresh board, keeps the latest session ref in step with state, exposes actions and composes the clock and saving hooks. Successful loads replace the game; failed loads publish notices. Exports and activations synchronize the clock first.

`session/browser-clock.ts` defines the 40ms scheduling interval and arithmetic over observed timestamps. `session/use-session-clock.ts` supplies observations, maintains visibility, schedules timeouts and removes pending work on effect cleanup. `session/browser-clock.test.ts` checks the arithmetic independently.

`session/fresh-board.ts` converts browser entropy into a valid board code, rejecting out-of-range candidates and an optional previous seed. `session/storage.ts` defines the preference key, version, default size, store interface, validators and best-score update. `session/use-saved-preferences.ts` obtains browser storage safely and writes changes in an effect.

`session/session.test.ts` covers state replacement, paused input, generations, repeated feedback events and completion handling. `session/storage.test.ts` uses in-memory and throwing stores to cover persistence decisions. Session module follows the exact call paths and state fields.

## Board directory

`board/Board.tsx` maps the immutable deck into cards. It derives a face-up set and a matched set, obtains the focus hook, exposes a remembered-focus method and supplies the `--grid-size` custom property. It keeps the activation callback stable while calling the latest controller action through a ref.

`board/Card.tsx` is memoized. It renders a native button, obtains its class and accessible description from `describeCard`, renders the face only when supplied and adds a matched mark for matched positions. It delegates navigation and focus to callbacks from the board.

`board/Face.tsx` converts a face design into inline SVG primitives. `board/face-design.ts` maps one of 128 face numbers to shape, marker, color, fill style, coordinates and label. `board/card-state.ts` derives a card's closed, revealed or matched description from supplied presentation data.

`board/keyboard.ts` computes arrow-navigation targets with edge stops and modifier handling. `board/use-board-focus.ts` owns the remembered position and DOM focus calls. `board/nearest-scroll.ts` remembers the viewport scroll position so focus can use nearest alignment after Chromium's automatic focus scrolling.

`board/board.css` owns the scrolling board viewport and grid tracks. `board/card.css` owns the button, concealed back, revealed/matched surfaces, corner mark and card transition. The directory's `keyboard.test.ts`, `card-state.test.ts` and `face-design.test.ts` check the numerical and descriptive helpers. Browser tests observe actual focus, artwork and scrolling.

## Controls and status

`controls/Controls.tsx` renders the grid-size select, New Game and Restart. It reads the size options from `GRID_SIZES`. `controls/control-labels.ts` owns the exact deal and reproduction control strings consumed by components and tests.

`controls/BoardCodeForm.tsx` renders the board-code field and submit button. Its input is keyed by generation, and successful submission moves focus to the load button because the old input is replaced. An invalid submission leaves the draft available for correction.

`controls/Reproduction.tsx` holds the snapshot textarea draft in local state, renders the details disclosure and export/load buttons, and shows the load notice and conditional Resume button outside the disclosure. It uses the game code and generation passed from the parent rather than reconstructing them.

`controls/control.css` defines the common control surface. `controls/controls.css` lays out deal controls. `controls/reproduction.css` lays out the disclosure, form rows, textarea and notice region.

`status/GameStatus.tsx` renders moves, pair progress, elapsed text, best moves and the completion paragraph. `status/status-labels.ts` owns statistic labels. `status/status.css` styles the statistic layout and completion treatment. The component receives the optional best as `number | undefined` and displays `none` when it is absent.

## Scripts directory

`scripts/replay.ts` is the command entry. It passes command-line arguments to `runReplay` and assigns the returned status to `process.exitCode`. `scripts/replay-cli.ts` handles one input path, caller-directory resolution, file reads, human-readable stderr failures and final snapshot output. `scripts/replay.test.ts` exercises the executable in child processes.

`scripts/source-files.ts` recursively reads ordinary files from a supplied folder and rejects links or special entries. `scripts/source-audit.test.ts` inspects packages, compiler settings, source length, unsafe constructs and selected effect boundaries. `scripts/source-conventions.test.ts` checks recognized exports/imports, yes-or-no naming, test names and environment reads.

These scripts are not imported by the application entry. Some import core functions because they are clients of the same public data behavior. That direction lets command-line replay reuse the rules without putting Node APIs into browser modules.

## Application-level test support

`tests/browser-test.ts` adapts Node tests to Playwright, manages browsers and contexts, records runtime versions, gathers page errors and provides artifact paths. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the built HTML over loopback. `tests/game-fixture.ts` contains public-control setup helpers, disk URLs and completion helpers.

`tests/deal-oracle.ts` independently computes a specified deal with BigInt. `tests/focus-bounds.ts`, `tests/readability.ts`, `tests/accessibility-tree.ts` and `tests/ui-snapshot.ts` provide focused measurement or comparison support. They are tools used by journeys, not application modules.

The many `.e2e.test.ts` files are grouped by the observable behavior they examine: controls, input, play, persistence, snapshots, lifecycle, clock edges, layout, motion, artwork, status, accessibility, touch and zoom. Test policy explains the runner and evidence boundaries instead of repeating every assertion here.

## Diagnostic entries and configured outputs

`art/index.html` and `art/face-sheet.tsx` form a separate face-sheet build with `art/face-sheet.css`. It imports the real card and design definitions to render every face at a controlled size. `vite.art.config.ts` writes this entry to `.art`.

`art/session/index.html` and `art/session/session-harness.tsx` form a separate lifecycle harness. It mounts `Game` beside an unmount button. `vite.session.config.ts` writes it to `.session`. The harness exists so the browser suite can measure cleanup rather than infer it from a page navigation.

The production build writes `dist/index.html`. Local dependencies live under `node_modules`; browser downloads, temporary browser files, npm cache and test work have separate ignored directories. `test-results` holds browser runtime and journey artifacts. These directories have operational roles but are not additional application source layers.

There is no generated route tree, backend, API client, asset service or utility framework to discover beyond this map. For command ordering see Build pipeline; for import and runtime separation see React boundaries.
import { useRef } from 'react';
import { Board } from './board/Board.tsx';
import { Controls } from './controls/Controls.tsx';
import { Reproduction } from './controls/Reproduction.tsx';
import { GameStatus } from './status/GameStatus.tsx';
import type { BoardFocus } from './board/Board.tsx';
import { useGame } from './session/use-game.ts';
import './game.css';

export function Game() {
  const controller = useGame();
  const { session } = controller;
  const { game } = session;
  const board = useRef<BoardFocus>(null);
  function resume(): void {
    board.current?.focusRemembered();
    controller.resume();
  }
  return (
    <main>
      <header>
        <p className="eyebrow">A little focus. A perfect pair.</p>
        <h1>Neon Pairs</h1>
      </header>
      <p className="intro">Reveal two cards. Match their shape and marker to keep the pair.</p>
      <Controls size={game.size} newGame={controller.newGame} restart={controller.restart} />
      <GameStatus
        game={game}
        best={session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]}
        celebration={session.celebration}
      />
      <p id="board-help" className="help">
        Use a pointer or Tab to enter the board. Arrow keys move between cards. Enter or Space
        reveals a card.
      </p>
      <div className="game-result">
        <p role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">
          <span key={session.announcement}>{session.feedback}</span>
        </p>
      </div>
      <Board key={session.generation} game={game} activate={controller.activate} ref={board} />
      <Reproduction
        game={game}
        generation={session.generation}
        exportSnapshot={controller.exportSnapshot}
        loadBoard={controller.loadBoard}
        loadSnapshot={controller.loadSnapshot}
        notice={session.loadNotice}
        paused={session.paused}
        resume={resume}
      />
    </main>
  );
}
import { useRef, useState } from 'react';
import { createGame } from '../game.ts';
import { parseBoardCode, isValidSize } from '../deck.ts';
import { decodeSnapshot, encodeSnapshot } from '../snapshot.ts';
import { freshBoardCode } from './fresh-board.ts';
import { activateSession, initialSession, replaceGame, SessionNotice } from './session.ts';
import { readPreferences } from './storage.ts';
import { browserStore, useSavedPreferences } from './use-saved-preferences.ts';
import { useSessionClock } from './use-session-clock.ts';
import type { Session } from './session.ts';

export function useGame() {
  const [store] = useState(browserStore);
  const [session, setSession] = useState(() => {
    const preferences = readPreferences(store);
    return initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences);
  });
  const current = useRef(session);

  function commit(next: Session): void {
    if (next === current.current) return;
    current.current = next;
    setSession(next);
  }

  const clock = useSessionClock(session, current, commit);
  useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences);

  function newGame(size = current.current.game.size): void {
    if (!isValidSize(size)) return;
    const next = createGame(freshBoardCode(size, current.current.game.seed));
    clock.reset();
    commit(replaceGame(current.current, next, false));
  }

  function restart(): void {
    clock.reset();
    commit(replaceGame(current.current, createGame(current.current.game.boardCode), false));
  }

  function notice(feedback: string): void {
    commit({
      ...current.current,
      feedback,
      loadNotice: feedback,
      announcement: current.current.announcement + 1,
    });
  }

  function loadBoard(code: string): boolean {
    code = code.trim();
    if (!parseBoardCode(code)) {
      notice(SessionNotice.invalidBoard);
      return false;
    }
    clock.reset();
    commit(replaceGame(current.current, createGame(code), false));
    return true;
  }

  function loadSnapshot(text: string): boolean {
    const game = decodeSnapshot(text);
    if (!game) {
      notice(SessionNotice.invalidSnapshot);
      return false;
    }
    clock.reset();
    commit(replaceGame(current.current, game, true));
    return true;
  }

  function exportSnapshot(): string {
    // Rendered state can trail the active clock by a tick.
    clock.synchronize();
    return encodeSnapshot(current.current.game);
  }

  function activate(index: number): void {
    clock.synchronize();
    commit(activateSession(current.current, index));
  }

  function resume(): void {
    clock.reset();
    commit({
      ...current.current,
      paused: false,
      feedback: '',
      loadNotice: '',
    });
  }

  return { session, newGame, restart, loadBoard, loadSnapshot, exportSnapshot, activate, resume };
}
import { activateCard, advanceGame, createGame, isWon } from '../game.ts';
import { SelectionKind } from '../selection.ts';
import { formatElapsed } from '../elapsed-time.ts';
import { rememberBest } from './storage.ts';
import type { GameState } from '../game.ts';
import type { Preferences } from './storage.ts';

export interface Session {
  readonly game: GameState;
  readonly paused: boolean;
  readonly generation: number;
  readonly feedback: string;
  readonly loadNotice: string;
  readonly announcement: number;
  readonly celebration: boolean;
  readonly preferences: Preferences;
}

export const SessionNotice = {
  loaded: 'Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.',
  loadedCompleted: 'Loaded completed snapshot.',
  invalidBoard: 'Invalid board code.',
  invalidSnapshot: 'Invalid snapshot.',
} as const;

export function initialSession(code: string, preferences: Preferences): Session {
  return {
    game: createGame(code),
    paused: false,
    generation: 0,
    feedback: '',
    loadNotice: '',
    announcement: 0,
    celebration: false,
    preferences,
  };
}

export function replaceGame(session: Session, game: GameState, imported: boolean): Session {
  const paused = imported && !isWon(game);
  const loadNotice = imported
    ? paused
      ? SessionNotice.loaded
      : SessionNotice.loadedCompleted
    : '';
  return {
    ...session,
    game,
    paused,
    generation: session.generation + 1,
    celebration: false,
    preferences: { ...session.preferences, size: game.size },
    // Only loads have a published status. A new deal clears the last turn result silently.
    announcement: imported ? session.announcement + 1 : session.announcement,
    feedback: loadNotice,
    loadNotice,
  };
}

export function tickSession(session: Session, generation: number, milliseconds: number): Session {
  if (session.generation !== generation || session.paused) return session;
  const game = advanceGame(session.game, milliseconds);
  return game === session.game ? session : { ...session, game };
}

export function activateSession(session: Session, index: number): Session {
  if (session.paused) return session;
  const game = activateCard(session.game, index);
  if (game === session.game) return session;
  if (game.selection.kind === SelectionKind.one) return { ...session, game };
  const won = isWon(game);
  const feedback = won
    ? `Pair found. All pairs found in ${game.moves} moves and ${formatElapsed(game.elapsedMs)}.`
    : game.selection.kind === SelectionKind.mismatch
      ? 'No match. Cards close after a short pause.'
      : `Pair found. ${game.matched.length / 2} ${game.matched.length === 2 ? 'pair' : 'pairs'} matched.`;
  const preferences = won
    ? rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)
    : session.preferences;
  return {
    ...session,
    game,
    feedback,
    announcement: session.announcement + 1,
    preferences,
    celebration: won,
  };
}
