docs/interface-review-checklist.md:5:A useful review follows a few populated journeys and checks source at the transitions. An empty board screenshot cannot show preserved drafts, matched-card focus or a stale timer after Restart. The checks below are grounded in the current source and specifications; links identify the separate policies for feature surfaces that do not exist yet.
docs/interface-review-checklist.md:16:The current page has no name editor, dialog or result table. A change introducing one has more scope than styling an existing control. Its relevant policy is linked below, and its current behavior has to be established from its own implementation.
docs/interface-review-checklist.md:30:The current buttons act immediately. A reviewer should not claim existing confirmation coverage from the presence of a leave policy elsewhere. Dialog policy records that separate feature boundary.
docs/interface-review-checklist.md:88:When a feature introduces name input, consult Text entry policy, Name length policy and Duplicate names policy. The existing code and JSON text fields do not establish those name checks. For new result content, consult Tables policy.
docs/adr-007-svg-faces.md:13:`face-design.ts` calculates the description from an integer face ID. `Face.tsx` turns that description into SVG geometry. Every face uses a `0 0 100 100` view box. The principal shape occupies the central area and the circular marker sits 40 units from the center in its assigned direction. Diagonal directions use `40 / Math.SQRT2`, so their distance is consistent with cardinal directions.
docs/spacing-scale.md:4:V09 in Visuals gives the positive layout values 4px, 6px, 8px, 12px, 16px, 24px and 32px, with zero resets and automatic centering allowed. Native-control internals are outside that rule. Borders, radii, outline geometry, font metrics and SVG coordinates have their own values. The distinction is useful because the source contains many lengths that are not layout spacing.
docs/spacing-scale.md:56:Margins do not always sum as independent strips. Block margins can collapse in ordinary flow, while flex and grid gaps do not collapse. A pixel estimate made by adding every listed margin can therefore differ from the actual bounding-box distance. The inventory tells where space is authored; browser measurement tells the resulting layout.
docs/purity-guide.md:13:The session also contains pure operations. `activateSession` adds feedback and completion preferences to a core transition, while `tickSession` gates a logical advance by generation and pause. Pure does not mean “must be in the top-level game directory”; it means the decision can be evaluated from explicit data without performing an external effect.
docs/incident-snapshot-rejects.md:37:Current `readMatched` checks each incoming index and counts occurrences of the associated face. Every represented face must occur twice. It preserves the incoming valid order in the returned list. `encodeSnapshot` later sorts a copy when producing readable text. No state mutation is needed merely to present the list consistently.
docs/acceptance.md:23:Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.
docs/acceptance.md:29:Play through completion and reset while checking Sound. Every action stays silent.
docs/adr-054-acceptance-journeys.md:19:A focused game test can prove that `createGame` returns zero moves and a closed selection. A session test can prove that a mismatched generation is ignored. The browser journey supplies the final connection: perform the mismatch, restart through the actual control, reveal a card and let earlier work become due. The newly revealed card must reflect the current game, not an old callback.
docs/retired-idea-online-play.md:13:This distinction was useful because it preserved the value of board codes even after the connected feature was retired. The board-code format remains a compact way to repeat a starting arrangement, not a room address or invitation token.
docs/retired-idea-online-play.md:21:The team did not choose a message protocol, room format, or hosting provider. Those would have been new implementation commitments for a feature the project had not approved. Retirement left the current app's simpler service boundary intact.
docs/retired-idea-online-play.md:61:This is not described as an online feature in disguise. The app does not send the artifacts, list recipients, or track another player's progress. It simply makes local state reproducible. The sharing FAQ covers these existing capabilities.
docs/retired-idea-online-play.md:63:The idea was retired because live connection would have required a new product and service design, while the immediate need was understandable local play and reliable issue reproduction. Roadmap notes retain the distinction between discussion and commitment. No account screen, remote message type, or future compatibility promise was reserved in the current implementation.
docs/pointer-and-touch.md:29:The result is a two-stage behavior. Focus memory may update during the press, without moving the target under the pointer. Completed activation is followed by nearest scrolling. A refactor that always scrolls in `onFocus` could pass centered-card click checks and still fail edge clicks. A refactor that removes the click scroll could preserve activation but leave the chosen card clipped.
docs/browser-test-guide.md:34:The `after` hook closes the normal browser, any lazily created visible-scrollbar browser, and the server. Tests creating an extra context themselves close it explicitly, as the phone completion journey does in a `finally` block. This is practical resource ownership, not an assumption that process exit will always clean up successfully.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:10:The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:14:Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.
docs/adr-011-storage-keys.md:27:The storage adapter exposed `getItem` and `setItem`, allowing a fake store to throw during tests. Parsing, access and writing could all fail without preventing the in-memory game from proceeding. Reading a versioned key therefore did not imply that persistence was always available. The browser origin still controlled access, and direct disk opening had browser-dependent storage behavior.
docs/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:13:`decodeSnapshot` treats parsed data as unknown. It checks the complete shape, version, code, bounded integer counters, matched positions and selection. Extra keys are rejected. Matched positions must be unique, in range and form whole face pairs. A pending mismatch needs two different unmatched positions whose faces differ, with remaining time from 1 through 800 whole milliseconds.
docs/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:15:The decoder also checks relationships. Moves must cover the matched pairs and a pending mismatch. An unstarted game has no progress. A started game with zero moves needs its first revealed card. These checks prevent combinations that contradict the current state rules without requiring an exhaustive reconstruction of earlier play. Snapshot selection notes explains the selection cases.
docs/board-keyboard-navigation.md:72:The helper leaves page scrolling to the browser. It does not freeze the outer document or always force the board to its top-left corner. Nearest means making the card visible with a small necessary movement, rather than centering every visited card. Tests check interior cards as well as corners because padding alone can hide a mid-board outline problem.
docs/disabled-state-guide.md:63:The current forms do not use `required`, a disabled submit button or `aria-invalid` as their validation mechanism. Their native length limits constrain editing, and the controller reports invalid content on action. Error display guide traces those outcomes and the preservation of drafts.
docs/disabled-state-guide.md:65:This describes the existing controls, not a new general rule that every possible action in a future feature is always enabled. The relevant question in review is which layer owns the reason an action cannot change state, and whether the element's semantics and focus behavior match that reason.
docs/game-state-model.md:83:A started zero-move game has one card revealed. Moves are at least matched pairs plus one for a pending mismatch; earlier misses explain larger counts. No positive time per move is required. Live timing may be fractional, with whole-millisecond conversion at serialization.
docs/private-browsing-notes.md:9:Chrome Help's “Browse in Incognito mode” describes site data as temporary during an Incognito session and removed when that session ends. Firefox Help's “How Private Windows protect you” similarly describes deleting session site data after all Private Windows close. These are lifetime descriptions, not guarantees that every site can always write under every privacy setting.
docs/private-browsing-notes.md:27:A store can also be obtainable while `getItem` or `setItem` throws. The reader and writer catch those failures independently. There is no need for the game to identify whether the cause is private browsing, a site setting or a browser policy. Storage failure policy covers the feature presentation and the current adapter's silent behavior.
docs/flaky-test-notes.md:52:`clock-edges.e2e.test.ts` chooses 1035ms and 330ms waits, both between ordinary render ticks. Export must include all active time and the correct pending interval. That test intentionally relies on synchronization. The idle-return tests intentionally avoid it until after the critical wait.
docs/test-policy.md:13:The architecture specification A10 asks for focused tests near behavior, independent literal generation vectors, transitions checked against stated rules and built HTML checked from disk as well as served. Those are different obligations because no single test environment can establish all of them.
docs/test-policy.md:41:Snapshot tests check outer keys, numeric bounds, matched-position consistency and each selection form. `snapshot-selection.test.ts` focuses on nested selection invariants. A selected index must name an available position, a mismatch must involve different faces and complete matched pairs must be represented together. The decoder reconstructs its deck from the code before checking these relationships.
docs/storage-failure-policy.md:9:For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.
docs/storage-failure-policy.md:21:The third operation is writing a serialized replacement. `writePreferences` encloses both serialization and `setItem` in its `try` block. A thrown error is swallowed so it cannot interrupt play. A browser may accept reads and refuse writes, so successful startup does not establish successful saving. Quota exhaustion is one possible write failure; browser policy is another.
docs/storage-failure-policy.md:73:These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. Storage testing guide extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.
docs/layout-grid.md:4:The layout has two width decisions. `main` keeps the document within the available page width and centers its content area. `.board-viewport` bounds the board's visible area, while `.board` can have a larger scrollable grid inside it. This arrangement lets a small board fit naturally and a large board keep useful card sizes. The related requirements are V02 through V05 and V19 in Visuals.

docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:5:The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:9:The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from Text entry policy. Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:45:The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. Error display guide provides the current feedback mechanics.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:49:Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.
docs/elapsed-time-rules.md:44:Every result includes a new clock observed at `now`, even when no duration was counted. Advancing the observation during inactivity is essential: the next active observation can then exclude the period spent waiting, hidden, or paused.
docs/storage-testing-guide.md:73:There is no useful assertion that the new board code must differ after every independent page load. Startup creates a fresh deal rather than restoring the old one, but a storage test can establish the intended state through cleared progress and retained preferences without depending on a random coincidence being impossible. New Game's seed handling is a separate behavior.
docs/voice-guide.md:44:The final turn's feedback combines the pair result with completion: “Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.” The visible banner uses a related sentence: “Every pair found in N moves and time. Well played.” Here `N` and `time` describe substitutions, not literal interface text. The banner and turn feedback serve different reading situations; copying one into the other without checking the component would lose that distinction.
docs/voice-guide.md:46:“Perfect” in the eyebrow is an atmospheric phrase about pairs. It is not a score classification. The implementation has moves, matched pairs, elapsed time and a local best move count, rather than grades such as excellent, average or poor. A release note or help paragraph that describes a “perfect rating” would create a feature the game does not have.
docs/randomness-policy.md:5:A new board needs an unpredictable seed. A board code, restart, imported snapshot and replay need the opposite property: a particular code always reconstructs the same deck. The implementation keeps those two tasks separate rather than letting a shuffle consult ambient state. Deck generation covers the deal algorithm as a format; this page concentrates on its source ownership and integration.
docs/randomness-policy.md:15:The fresh-board module uses a one-element `Uint32Array` and `crypto.getRandomValues`. Its possible raw values span the unsigned 32-bit range, with `UINT32_RANGE` set to `2 ** 32`. The allowed seed range is defined in `deck.ts` by `SEED_MAX = 2_147_483_646`. Valid codes use positive seeds, so the transformation adds one after taking a remainder.
docs/randomness-policy.md:17:The module computes `RANDOM_LIMIT = Math.floor(UINT32_RANGE / SEED_MAX) * SEED_MAX`. With the current values the limit is `4_294_967_292`. A draw below that limit is accepted; one at or above it is retried. Thus each allowed remainder has the same number of accepted raw values. The last four unsigned values do not enter the modulo mapping.

docs/module-layout-policy.md:11:The session directory has a different responsibility. It connects rules to React state, browser observations and saved preferences. A feature lives in src/game/FEATURE/, and its rules live in src/game/FEATURE/rules.ts, which imports neither React nor any browser global. That placement gives a reader a predictable starting point for a feature's decisions, with the integration code close enough to inspect alongside them.
docs/module-layout-policy.md:13:This convention applies to feature work; existing behaviors also use other filenames. The current core is in `game.ts`, `deck.ts`, `selection.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts` and `replay.ts` directly under `src/game`. The board already uses focused names such as `keyboard.ts` and `card-state.ts`.
docs/module-layout-policy.md:35:Technology specification T06 sets an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 authored TypeScript lines per file. The source audit checks the ceiling across `src`, `scripts`, `tests` and `art`. The aim is a reading aid, not a reason to scatter every function into a separate module.

docs/release-notes-1-2.md:35:The large-board review made near-neighbor comparison important. A circle and triangle with the same top marker were easy to tell apart; a solid and outline square with a diagonal marker required a more careful drawing. Today's SVG keeps the main shape within the central portion of a `100 100` view box and draws a marker above it with a separating background stroke. docs/architecture.md:46:- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.
docs/architecture.md:48:- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.
docs/architecture.md:52:- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

docs/focus-policy.md:11:A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. docs/research-phone-usage.md:67:The phone study supported three concrete interpretations of usability: a scroll must not spend a move, the board's overflow must not drag the whole document sideways, and returning from an interruption must have a coherent time meaning. docs/snapshot-selection-notes.md:58:The `one` variant has exactly `kind` and `index`. That index must pass availability. The returned object contains only the known fields, preserving the numeric position.
docs/snapshot-selection-notes.md:66:The exact key set is `kind`, `first`, `second`, `remainingMs`. Both positions need to be available, and they must be distinct. docs/text-entry-policy.md:9:A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:11:The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:79:The current code's strongest relevant lesson is explicit boundaries: BoardCodeForm submits a draft, the controller validates, replacement updates the model, and rendered controls follow that model. docs/reproducibility.md:10:- D01 - Use `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and `seed` is an integer from `1` through `2147483646`. Use decimal digits without leading zeros. The parser accepts exactly this form. Trim surrounding whitespace in the Board code control before parsing.
docs/reproducibility.md:11:- D02 - Version `np1` fixes the generation algorithm below. The same code produces the same deck in every supported runtime. Changing generation requires another version. Time, animation and other random draws can't change this deck.
docs/reproducibility.md:17:- D03 - Start the Park-Miller generator at `state = seed`. Each draw sets `state = (state * 16807) % 2147483647`. Use exact integer arithmetic. Seed 1 starts with states `16807`, `282475249`, `1622650073`, `984943658` and `1144108930`.
docs/reproducibility.md:18:- D04 - Create the deck as `[0, 0, 1, 1, ...]` through face `N * N / 2 - 1`. Shuffle from index `N * N - 1` down to `1`. At index `i`, draw `j` in `0..i` and swap positions `i` and `j`.
docs/reproducibility.md:26:- D05 - Encode progress as a JSON object with exactly `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. `version` is `1`. `matched` is an array of matched position indices. Derive the deck, pair count and completion from these fields.
docs/reproducibility.md:36:- D06 - Validate the complete object before replacing the game. Reject unknown keys. Require unique in-range matched indices containing whole face pairs. Selection indices must be in range and unmatched. A mismatch needs distinct indices with different faces and an integer `remainingMs` from `1` through `800`. Completion requires a closed selection.
docs/reproducibility.md:37:- D07 - Require boolean `started` and nonnegative safe integers for `moves` and `elapsedMs`. Reject `elapsedMs` above `359999999` and `moves` above `999999`. Apply the move cap to saved best scores too. Require at least one move per matched pair and one further move for a pending mismatch. If `started` is false, require zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matches and a closed selection. A started game with zero moves requires one revealed card. Import of unfinished progress pauses the clock and pending mismatch until Resume. Completed imports stay completed without a pause.
docs/reproducibility.md:49:- D08 - Encode a single deal as `{version: 1, boardCode, actions: [{atMs, index}], endMs}`. Require exactly these fields and exactly `atMs` and `index` per action. Indices must be in range. Times are nonnegative safe integers. Action times must be nondecreasing. If actions exist, `endMs` must be at least the final action time. Equal-time actions keep array order.
docs/reproducibility.md:50:- D09 - Start from the code's hidden deal. Advance active time to each action's `atMs` before activating its index, then advance to `endMs`. Resolve a mismatch whose interval ends exactly at an action time before that action. Apply the game rules to ignored activation too. Cap replayed elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds as R07 requires. Action times and `endMs` keep the nonnegative safe integer range in D08.
docs/reproducibility.md:62:- D10 - Limit snapshot JSON to `65536` UTF-8 bytes. Limit replay JSON to `1048576` UTF-8 bytes and `10000` actions. Reject malformed JSON and unsupported format versions. For snapshots, inconsistent data means a violation of D05, D06 or D07. For replays, it means a violation of D08 or D09. For board codes, validate D01. Validation checks these stated constraints, without requiring a reconstructed history of earlier turns. Invalid board codes and snapshots keep the current browser game. Invalid replay files are rejected by the CLI and game core.
docs/target-size-policy.md:9:The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.
docs/target-size-policy.md:73:For a new feature review, a concise measurement record can identify the viewport, the control's role and name, its width and height and whether it is fully reachable. The record is most useful alongside the rendered layout, because it can reveal that a formally large button is covered by another element or forced beyond the page edge. This is observation of the target in context, not a second numerical policy.
docs/meeting-notes-accessibility.md:21:The review rejected the idea that adding descriptive hidden text is always an access improvement. Description can disclose information that the game is deliberately withholding. The correct question is whether the player receives the same currently available information through the accessible representation.
docs/audio-research-notes.md:63:`GameStatus.tsx` displays a paragraph beginning “Every pair found in” with final moves and elapsed time. The completed board remains visible with checks. The normal status fields remain available. The session feedback for the final match combines the pair result and completion, rather than treating them as unrelated moments.
docs/research-playtest-spring.md:49:In the sessions, several people paused after the last pair and looked at their result before touching another control. An ephemeral message would have required them to catch the exact moment of completion. The current banner remains visible with moves and time after its optional single pulse.
docs/best-score-records.md:69:Activating a position on an already completed imported game does not turn it into a new completion event. Every valid position is matched, so `activateCard` returns the same game and the session exits before record handling.
docs/adr-044-no-routing.md:21:Browser Back and modifier combinations also retain ordinary browser meanings because the board handles only its stated keys. Introducing a navigation framework would add another consumer of history without a required screen transition to justify it. ADR 003 covers the delivery boundary.
docs/known-issues.md:6:## Reviewed JSON fixtures are required for the complete suite
docs/known-issues.md:40:The specification expects the browser's normal context menu and no card activation when that menu opens. The browser suite covers right-click behavior, completed taps, canceled input paths and touch scrolling. It explicitly leaves confirmation of real touch long press to acceptance because automated browsers cannot produce the required native gesture reliably.
docs/replay-format.md:24:All action times, action indices and `endMs` must be nonnegative safe integers. Positions also need to be smaller than the generated deck length. Action times are nondecreasing, and no action can occur after `endMs`. Object-key order is immaterial, but action-array order is part of the replay's meaning.
docs/selection-state.md:41:| Completed game | `closed` | Every position |
docs/selection-state.md:103:Parsed JSON needs runtime checks. `readSelection` in `snapshot-selection.ts` checks each alternative's exact fields. A one-card index must be a nonnegative safe integer in range and absent from matched. Mismatch requires two such distinct indices with different face values and an integer remainder from 1 through 800. Closed has only its discriminant.
docs/snapshot-format.md:8:`SNAPSHOT_VERSION` is `1`, and `SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES` is `65_536`. The required root fields are listed by `SNAPSHOT_KEYS`. There are exactly seven:
docs/snapshot-format.md:67:`one` means that a first eligible card has been revealed. The index must be inside the generated deck and absent from `matched`. This first reveal does not cost a move. In particular, `started: true`, `moves: 0`, no matches and a `one` selection is the normal state immediately after starting play.
docs/snapshot-format.md:75:Every matched index is a nonnegative safe integer smaller than the deck length. It must appear only once. The decoder counts generated face identities at those positions and requires every represented face to occur twice. An empty array is valid; an even number of positions is necessary but insufficient.
docs/snapshot-format.md:101:When `started` is false, all progress must be initial: zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matched positions and a closed selection. This prevents an object from combining hidden elapsed progress with an unstarted clock. It also ensures that importing an unstarted deal has a coherent state to resume.
docs/snapshot-format.md:122:Every failed branch returns `null`. The function does not expose a partial state or structured error. Its caller cannot distinguish a bad counter from a malformed selection by inspecting the return value. Current browser messaging is described in Import safety.
docs/snapshot-format.md:144:`hasExactKeys` combines an `Object.keys` count with `Object.hasOwn` for each required key. It does not care about enumeration order. At this string boundary the input has already been produced by `JSON.parse`; the helper is not a general schema engine or a tokenizer that remembers duplicate property occurrences. The same helpers serve replay parsing with different field lists and limits.
docs/native-controls-guide.md:58:A disclosure leaves the surrounding document operable and expands in flow. It is not equivalent to a modal overlay. That distinction matters when reading a feature description: choosing a different native element changes more than a border shape or animation.
docs/native-controls-guide.md:84:The source does not contain a component library or a custom form abstraction that all new controls must use. Shared labels and CSS are small local tools. ADR 006 is the decision reference, while Architecture explains the separation between browser effects and pure game behavior.
docs/board-size-catalogue.md:39:This is the first size at which remembering only a shape becomes insufficient across the complete deck. The game does not change its comparison rule to compensate: exact face equality has always been the criterion. Pair identity explains the dimensions that distinguish faces.
docs/board-size-catalogue.md:103:Every option uses the same two-card attempts, 800 active millisecond mismatch interval, first-reveal clock start, and matched-coverage completion. Scrolling preserves row-order positions. The seven values form the supported catalogue; arbitrary even side lengths are not accepted by the parser or size guard.
docs/regression-catalogue.md:58:The snapshot unit suite checks export after 0.75ms of a miss and again with 0.25ms left. The result must decode successfully and remain within one millisecond of the active state. The browser fractional test exercises the same boundary through the UI. A full round trip from an ordinary integer time would not cover this edge.
docs/regression-catalogue.md:84:The distinction between ordinary generation checks and rare-branch vectors is useful beyond this bug. Counting two of each face proves deck composition. It says nothing about the exact ordering required for a reproducible board code. A format change cannot be hidden behind a pair-count assertion.
docs/adr-028-prettier.md:25:A hand-maintained style guide would have required reviewers to enforce mechanical choices and authors to remember them across several file types. A more elaborate linting system could have combined style and semantic rules, but that would introduce a different configuration surface. The current formatter supplies the narrow mechanical function the project actually uses.
docs/adr-053-docs-in-repo.md:9:Repository documentation was chosen because the game has precise rules that are not obvious from a screenshot. The mismatch interval is active time, Restart repeats a code, unfinished imports pause, and a closed card must not expose identity. These details deserve readable explanations rather than only test assertions or comments scattered through components.
docs/adr-025-reduced-motion.md:21:The browser preference is already a user-controlled signal and works for the offline file without storing a second application setting. A game-level toggle would have duplicated that preference and added another persistence question. Treating motion as required feedback would also have made the reduced presentation less informative.
docs/README.md:44:Every project document, by area. Project-wide policies apply to all new work, including work that doesn't mention them.
docs/README.md:125:- persistence-envelope.md: The feature JSON envelope and its distinction from the existing versioned preference aggregate.
docs/README.md:127:- storage-failure-policy.md: Unavailable-storage behavior, feature feedback and the current adapter’s catch boundaries.
docs/README.md:149:- module-layout-policy.md: Behavior ownership, dependency direction and feature placement in the game source.

item.aggregated_output: # Focus policy This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen. Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things. ## Existing page and future screens `Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen. A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists. The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. Dialog policy covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus. ## Initial load is quiet The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method. The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board. A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing. ## Deal actions retain their location New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call. The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms. A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place. Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. Error display guide follows those cases in detail. ## Remembered board focus Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`. Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched. Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. Board keyboard navigation provides the calculations and edge behavior. ## Resume transfers before removal Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target. In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices. The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment. The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location. ## Visible focus and scroll clearance `game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area. The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail. `useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible. The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately. ## Focus is not completion feedback Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched. Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched. These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries. ## Review evidence The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring. A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. Interface review checklist gathers these journeys with layout and input checks. For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior. # Announcements policy This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering. The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards. ## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source. Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader. ## Session data behind the paragraph The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `{session.feedback}`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text. The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it. A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. ## Turn results `activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal. After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications. | Result | Text produced by the session | | --- | --- | | First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` | | Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` | | Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` | | Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` | Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count. A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. Screen reader notes follows those two sources in a complete game. ## Consecutive identical results Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them. The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity. The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card. There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game. ## Changes that stay quiet `tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause. Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result. New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load. Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains. ## Load outcomes share the publication path The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again. For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch. Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel. Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. Reproduction panel and Focus policy describe those effects independently of event publication. ## Completion and persistent reading GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time. The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game. A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did. ## Automated evidence `session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser. `tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure. The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role. The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance. ## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text. For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page.
